content.title: Where and What Time to Watch the Artemis II Splashdown on Friday, April 10, 2026
content.text: With the 10-day mission of Artemis II nearly complete, the four astronauts aboard the Orion spacecraft are quickly approaching their return back to Earth. How to WatchWatch NBC Nightly News with Tom Llamas nightly at 6:30/5:30C on NBC.Here's everything you should know about the Artemis splashdown — including when and where it will happen, and how to tune in to see the incredible event unfold live for yourself.RELATED: NBC News' Tom Costello Compares the Artemis II Mission to the Back To the Future MovieWhat time is the Artemis II landing?Artemis II's Orion spacecraft is scheduled to splash down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego, California, at approximately 8:07 p.m. ET on Friday, April 10, 2026.The return of Artemis II to Earth will be covered by NBC News and can be viewed here. Viewers can also tune into NASA's YouTube live stream of the event beginning at 6:30 p.m. ET by clicking here.According to NASA, a series of parachutes will be deployed to help with the safe return of NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, and Christina Koch, along with CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Jeremy Hansen."Once safely through the heat of reentry, the cover that protected the spacecraft’s forward bay will be jettisoned to make way for a series of parachutes to deploy — two drogue parachutes that will slow the capsule down to about 307 miles per hour, followed by three pilot parachutes that will pull out the final three main parachutes," NASA stated on its website. "These will slow Orion down to approximately 17 mph for a splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, where NASA and U.S. Navy personnel will be waiting for them, concluding the Artemis II mission."RELATED: When and Where Will Artemis II's Orion Capsule Land After Its Moon Mission?When did Artemis II launch?The Artemis II mission launched on April 1, 2026 from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Shortly after launch, the Orion space capsule detached itself from its rockets and began its flight around the moon and back.Since its launch, the team set a record for the farthest distance humans have ever traveled from Earth — 252,756 miles, set on April 6.How fast is Artemis II going?Upon reentry into the Earth's atmosphere, the Orion capsule is expected to reach speeds in excess of 25,000 miles per hour before splashing down at the relatively slow speed of just 17 miles per hour.During its spaceflight, Artemis II cruised through outer space at about 17,000 miles per hour, according to USA Today.Some of the most difficult parts of the journey are still to come.Re-entry is is particularly risky as spacecrafts can be exposed to temperatures of 5,000 degrees Fahrenheit, according to NBC News. And as for the Artemis II mission, the Orion spacecraft's heat shield, which protects astronauts from extreme temperatures, has flaws. RELATED: All the Shows NBC Has Renewed in 2026NASA planned a modified reentry path for the Orion to try minimize the risks.As the Orion returns through Earth’s atmosphere on Friday night, it will encounter temperatures of about 3,000 degrees Fahrenheit, according to NASA. The Artemis II team must enter the Earth's atmosphere at the correct angle to avoid damaging the heat shield.“If we stick to the new re-entry path that NASA has planned, then this heat shield will be safe to fly,” American astronaut Reid Wiseman said during a July media event.
